spec.title: Dry-run: a background job queue
spec.intro: About 5 minutes. The interesting part isn't the queue — it's making the worker safe to run twice.

steps.title: Enqueue is fire-and-forget from the caller's view
steps.explain: The request handler's job is to persist the work and return fast — the caller should never wait on the actual processing. Everything after this is invisible to the user who triggered it.
steps.saysOutLoud: The request path only has to guarantee the job is durably queued, not that it's done.

steps.title: A naive worker — breaks the moment it crashes mid-job
steps.explain: This looks fine until the process dies between 'do the work' and 'mark done'. The queue never saw an ack, redelivers the job, and if the work wasn't idempotent — like charging a card — it happens twice.

steps.title: Fix: make the handler itself idempotent
steps.explain: Rather than trying to make delivery exactly-once — which distributed queues generally can't promise — make redelivery harmless. A processed-set check plus atomic insert means a duplicate delivery is a no-op, so at-least-once delivery is fine.
steps.saysOutLoud: I don't fight the queue's at-least-once semantics — I make the handler idempotent instead.

steps.title: Visibility timeout, not a manual lock
steps.explain: While a worker holds a job it's invisible to other consumers for a bounded window. If the worker dies without acking, the job silently reappears after the timeout — no separate heartbeat or lock table needed for the common case.

steps.title: Retry with backoff, then dead-letter
steps.explain: Same shape as any retry policy: transient errors get exponential backoff, and a job that keeps failing moves to a dead-letter queue rather than looping forever and starving the main queue of throughput.

steps.title: The broker holds durability, not the app
steps.explain: SQS, Redis Streams, or Kafka persist the queue itself — the app process holds nothing across a restart. This is what makes 'the worker crashed' a survivable event instead of data loss: the job is sitting in the broker whether or not any worker is currently alive to pop it.

steps.title: Ordering is per-partition, not global
steps.explain: Workers scale horizontally by adding more consumers, which means global ordering is gone by default. If a job type genuinely needs order — events for one user, say — key the partition by user id so all of that user's jobs land on the same worker.

spec.closing: If they ask 'why not just a cron job': cron re-runs on a schedule regardless of backlog size and has no natural backpressure — a queue lets producers and consumers scale independently, and a slow spike just grows the queue depth instead of overlapping runs.
